messages.subject: Re: 4way mapping
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan

I'm Taslima, a graduate student from Tom's Lab. I was playing on this 4way cross that Tom described and have converted r/qtl genoprob for r/qtl2 format but when I was running calc_kinship I realize 4way cross is not supported to calculate kinship for r/qtl2.
Any thought?

Here is my code:

datmap<-pull.map(dataIM)
probs <- vector("list", length(datmap))

nmap <- vector("list", length(datmap))

n.ind <- nind(data)
chrnames <- chrnames(data)
is_x_chr <- logical(length = length(chrnames))
names(is_x_chr)<-chrnames
alleles<-as.vector(c("A","B","C","D"))

names(probs) <- names(datmap)
attr(probs, "is_x_chr") <- is_x_chr
attr(probs, "crosstype") <- "4way"
attr(probs,"alleles") <-alleles
attr(probs,"alleleprobs")<-logical(1)
attr(probs,"class")<-c("calc_genoprob" ,"list")

for (i in 1:length(probs)) {
  arr<-dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob
  flat<-adply(arr,2)
  column.names <- c("AC","BC","AD","BD")
  row.names <- rownames(dataIM$pheno)
  matrix.names <- attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$dimnames[[2]] #gsub("(\\.)[A-z][A-z]","",colnames(test),perl = T)
  dim<-attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$dim

  narr <- array(unlist(flat[,-1]),dim = c(dim[1],dim[3],dim[2]),dimnames = list(row.names,column.names,matrix.names))
  probs[[names(probs)[i]]]<-narr

  nmap[[names(probs)[i]]] <-unlist(as.data.frame(attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$map)[1,])

}

attr(probs, "map") <- nmap

kinship <- calc_kinship(probs)

And the error is:

Error in .genoprob_to_alleleprob(attr(probs, "crosstype"), aperm(probs[[chr]],  :
  cross type not yet supported.

Best,
Taslima

We've resequenced the population and our markers are all fully informative and phased AB x CD.  I've been running scanone in r/qtl for some preliminary mapping. It would be nice if we could do some genomescans that allow control for background residual genetic variation.  However, my understanding is that cim and stepwiseqtl in r/qtl have not been implemented for the 4way design. I'm wondering whether it would be helpful to consider loco scans using r/qtl2.  Has anyone worked with a 4-way in r/qtl2?  I tried to use "convert2cross2" but it is not working for 4way designs.  Any thoughts or suggestions on moving to r/qtl2?
>
> Best,
> Tom
>

Hi Karl

I have few more queries for this 4-way cross issue:

1. The plant we are working on is a tetraploid therefore to match multiple sets of chromosomes we marked chromosomes as 1N, 1K, 2N, 2K, which makes each chr  as string, not numeric. So, when I'm going to plot the result of scanone in rqtl2 I got the following error

"Error in plot.window(...) : need finite 'xlim' values"

Do you thing changing the chr names into numerics will help? something like this :

chrnames <- seq(1:18)

In that case do you thing I need to change marker names too?

2. I also tried find_peaks and then I realize the way I converted genotype probability rqtl2 can not distinguish between pseudomarker and real marker. There are multiple pseudomarkers as loc.xx which may present for all 18 chr so I'm getting the following error:

Error in `levels<-`(`*tmp*`, value = if (nl == nL) as.character(labels) else paste0(labels,  :
  factor level [2] is duplicated

Do you think I should change the name of these pseudomarkers according to their chr?

Here, I'm attaching my cross object which is "dataIM" and following is my code to convert  data for rqtl2 and run scanone:

https://drive.google.com/open?id=1mnbW6rU8on3MvyThy-_ogmYuOBY_GV1v

datmap<-pull.map(dataIM)
probs <- vector("list", length(datmap))

nmap <- vector("list", length(datmap))

n.ind <- nind(dataIM)
chrnames <- chrnames(dataIM)

is_x_chr <- logical(length = length(chrnames))
names(is_x_chr)<-chrnames
alleles<-as.vector(c("A","B","C","D"))

names(probs) <- names(datmap)
attr(probs, "is_x_chr") <- is_x_chr
attr(probs, "crosstype") <- "4way"
attr(probs,"alleles") <-alleles
attr(probs,"alleleprobs")<-logical(1)
attr(probs,"class")<-c("calc_genoprob" ,"list")

for (i in 1:length(probs)) {
  arr<-dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob
  flat<-adply(arr,2)
  column.names <- c("AC","BC","AD","BD")
  row.names <- rownames(dataIM$pheno)
  matrix.names <- attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$dimnames[[2]] #gsub("(\\.)[A-z][A-z]","",colnames(test),perl = T)
  dim<-attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$dim

  narr <- array(unlist(flat[,-1]),dim = c(dim[1],dim[3],dim[2]),dimnames = list(row.names,column.names,matrix.names))
  probs[[names(probs)[i]]]<-narr

  nmap[[names(probs)[i]]] <-unlist(as.data.frame(attributes(dataIM$geno[[names(probs)[i]]]$prob)$map)[1,])

}

attr(probs, "map") <- nmap

kinship <- calc_kinship(probs,use_allele_probs = F)
kinship_loco <- calc_kinship(probs,use_allele_probs = F,type = "loco")

pheno<-as.matrix(dataIM$pheno[,-3])
rownames(pheno)<-rownames(dataIM$pheno)

out<-scan1(probs, pheno ,kinship = kinship_loco)
out_perm<-scan1perm(probs, pheno ,kinship = kinship_loco,cores = 3,n_perm = 100)
summary(out_perm,alpha = 0.05)

find_peaks(out,threshold = 4.99,map = nmap)

Best,
Taslima

The chromosome names are stored as character strings not integers, so I don't think this is the cause of the problem.
They're actually taken from the names of the components of the map object.

My guess is that you've got some NAs for marker positions in the map?

> 2. I also tried find_peaks and then I realize the way I converted genotype probability rqtl2 can not distinguish between pseudomarker and real marker. There are multiple pseudomarkers as loc.xx which may present for all 18 chr so I'm getting the following error:

>   factor level [2] is duplicated
>
>
> Do you think I should change the name of these pseudomarkers according to their chr?
>

Yes, I would make sure that all pseudomarkers have unique names. They end up as rownames in the output of scan1() and so need to be distinct.

karl

messages.subject: QTL x environment interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi all:

My group is interested in studying gene-by-environment interaction for quantitative traits.  We often grow lines from various mapping populations in multiple environments and want to test how the additive effect of a QTL changes by condition.  We primarily work with plants and so often have inbred lines or can clonally propagate genotypes (plants are GREAT!) and can easily grow them across environments. I think it’s probably best to think of these as repeated measures experiments.  In several past projects we’ve studied QTL x E in RILs by growing lines in two environments and map on the average of RIL line means and on the difference of RIL line means.  We think of the average as an estimate of G (or the constitutive/stable QTL) and the difference as an estimate of the GxE or environmentally sensitive QTL.

However, our projects keep expanding and now we are looking at genotypes across much more complex environments – often involving 10 or more conditions.  Here, the average and difference are not as elegant of an approach. In a few cases we’ve considered models that fit the conditions as additive and interactive covariates using rqtl.  So, something like y ~ u + QTL + condition + QTL*condition + error using scanone.  We implement this by “stacking” the phenotypes and genotypes in our rqtl input files and include a column indicating condition.  This works, but is probably not ideal, as the model doesn’t incorporate the fact that the same RIL lines are grown in the two environments.  We’ve been brainstorming running similar models in Rqtl2 but including the kinship matrix in this model.  Here, we’d be able to incorporate the repeated measures nature of the experiment as indicated in the kinship matrix.  So, something like y~ u + QTL + condition + QTL*condition + kinship + error.  I realize that we wouldn’t be able to model polygenic*condition interaction, but this seems a step up from ignoring the fact we are growing the same genotypes over and over again.

Does this seem like a sound direction? Can we stack phenotypes and genotypes like this in Rqtl2?

Best,

Tom

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] QTL x environment interaction
messages.body_plain:
You can fit this sort of model in R/qtl2, using scan1() with a kinship matrix and addcovar or intcovar.
But with 10 conditions, you maybe want to treat condition as a random effect, and we don't currently have the ability to fit such  linear mixed models this in R/qtl2.

I think the main uses of R/qtl (1 and 2) are
  - diagnostics for genotype data
  - calculating genotype probabilities from marker genotype data
  - performing genome scans with very simple linear or mixed models
  - visualizing the results

Ultimately, I'd like to include the ability to have covariates be random effects, but more generally I think it'll be common to find cases where people want to fit more complicated models than what we've implemented. But if you can figure out how to fit your model at a single locus, you can embed that within a for() loop and fit it at each of the loci. Then cram the results back into something that the R/qtl (1 or 2) plotting functions can deal with.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] QTL x environment interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl:

Thanks for the response.  We have a variety of GxE cases - in some situations the environments are unordered conditions/sites that differ in many regards and that might make sense as fixed effects. In other cases, it might be possible to order them and think of them as a continuous gradient (e.g. latitude or a temperature gradient).  We rarely have the sampling of environments such that I've implemented E as a random effect, but Saunak Sen and I have talked about this a bit.

I guess one option would be to consider running analyses in something like lme4qtl - are you familiar with it?

https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12859-018-2057-x

This allows fixed and random effects, including kinship type structures.  Most of our populations have dense markers - presumably we can do marker by marker tests with kinship and random effects.....this might be something to try.

Tom

This works, but is probably not ideal, as the model doesn’t incorporate the fact that the same RIL lines are grown in the two environments.  We’ve been brainstorming running similar models in Rqtl2 but including the kinship matrix in this model.  Here, we’d be able to incorporate the repeated measures nature of the experiment as indicated in the kinship matrix.  So, something like y~ u + QTL + condition + QTL*condition + kinship + error.  I realize that we wouldn’t be able to model polygenic*condition interaction, but this seems a step up from ignoring the fact we are growing the same genotypes over and over again.
> >
> >
> >
> > Does this seem like a sound direction? Can we stack phenotypes and genotypes like this in Rqtl2?
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > Tom

In other cases, it might be possible to order them and think of them as a continuous gradient (e.g. latitude or a temperature gradient).  We rarely have the sampling of environments such that I've implemented E as a random effect, but Saunak Sen and I have talked about this a bit.
>
> I guess one option would be to consider running analyses in something like lme4qtl - are you familiar with it?
>
> https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12859-018-2057-x
>
> This allows fixed and random effects, including kinship type structures.  Most of our populations have dense markers - presumably we can do marker by marker tests with kinship and random effects.....this might be something to try.

> Tom
>

> >
> > I think the main uses of R/qtl (1 and 2) are
> >   - diagnostics for genotype data
> >   - calculating genotype probabilities from marker genotype data
> >   - performing genome scans with very simple linear or mixed models
> >   - visualizing the results
> >
> > Ultimately, I'd like to include the ability to have covariates be random effects, but more generally I think it'll be common to find cases where people want to fit more complicated models than what we've implemented. But if you can figure out how to fit your model at a single locus, you can embed that within a for() loop and fit it at each of the loci. Then cram the results back into something that the R/qtl (1 or 2) plotting functions can deal with.
> >

I realize that we wouldn’t be able to model polygenic*condition interaction, but this seems a step up from ignoring the fact we are growing the same genotypes over and over again.
> > >
